evidence.text: The page shows bronze, seal, and standard forms. Its account treats 自 and 心 as semantic elements: 自 represents the nose, while 心 reflects the ancient belief that breathing originated in the heart. This supports a semantic-component analysis, not 自 as phonetic.

This is an early lexicographic phonetic analysis, but it is not independent proof of the graph’s original construction; paleographic accounts disagree, treating both parts semantically and the lower shape as later regularization.

evidence.source: Dong Chinese
evidence.text: This account describes 息 as breath going into the nose, with the lower breath strokes later reanalyzed as 心. It labels a displayed bronze form Late Shang (~1100 BCE), a seal form Shuowen (~100 CE), and a clerical form Eastern Han (25–220 CE). It also reproduces Shuowen’s “息，喘也。从心，从自，自亦聲,” which assigns 自 a phonetic role. These are the page’s account and labels; the page does not provide an independently dated inscription citation in the inspected text.

evidence.source: Japanese National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics entry reproduced by Kotobank
evidence.field: 精選版 日本国語大辞典: dated examples; 字通: graphic and semantic account
evidence.text: The entry gives dated Japanese examples for readings and uses of 息: breath in a Nihon Shoki example dated 720, breathing in a Man’yōshū example assigned to the 8th century, offspring/son in an example from 1031, interest in a Shoku Nihongi example dated 743, and rest in an example assigned to 1384. These attest Japanese lexical uses and do not establish the chronology of the Chinese character’s senses. The accompanying 字通 account analyzes 自＋心 as nose plus heart and cites the Zhuangzi, but this is an interpretation, not independent paleographic proof.
